extracted.intended_audience: systematic reviewers, researchers, decision-makers, research funders, journal editors and research ethics committees in health/medical research
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for detecting, preventing and dealing with publication and related dissemination biases when conducting systematic reviews and evidence synthesis in health research. Covers search strategy, registration, statistical methods, qualitative assessment of risk, and implications for decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider potential for publication and related bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential problem of publication and related bias should be taken into consideration by all who are involved in evidence-based decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that dissemination of research findings is likely to be biased and that the actual impact of such bias may be uncertain and context-dependent (basic research, observational studies, clinical trials). Incorporate this consideration into review planning, interpretation and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support prospective research registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers, research funders and RECs at the national and international level should continue to support the development of prospective research registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prospective universal registration of all studies at inception is described as the ideal solution to publication bias. Note that voluntary registration is usually incomplete and past efforts have focused on phase III/IV trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement research open-access policy / right to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Open access policy/regulation and improved research funders’ guidelines (right to publication) help address dissemination bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage open-access databases maintained by regulatory bodies, societies or sponsors and policies guaranteeing dissemination rights to reduce non-publication and limited access to results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endorse and use practical reporting guidelines; report all measured outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical and sound reporting guidelines should be endorsed by journals, and authors should report all measured outcomes in their studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endorsement of reporting guidelines can improve completeness of reporting and reduce outcome reporting bias. Review authors should expect and require full outcome reporting when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct thorough literature searches including registers, grey/unpublished/non-English studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible, a thorough literature search should be conducted in systematic reviews to identify all relevant studies. Registers of clinical trials and available databases of unpublished studies should be routinely searched for relevant clinical trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search strategies should routinely include trial registries, grey literature sources, databases of unpublished studies and non-English-language sources as appropriate to the topic; only 18% of treatment reviews searched prospective research registers in one assessment, indicating underuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not routinely exclude unpublished studies or conference abstracts; assess their quality equally
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic reviews should not routinely exclude unpublished studies or conference abstracts. The quality of unpublished studies or abstracts should be assessed using the same criteria as for formally published studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of unpublished material can reduce bias, but reviewers must apply the same methodological quality assessments and consider limitations of abstracts/unpublished reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and address outcome reporting bias; contact original authors for missing outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome reporting bias has been confirmed by new evidence and should be seriously considered in systematic reviews. When relevant studies cannot be included owing to a lack of data on relevant outcomes, original authors should be contacted to clarify whether the outcome was actually measured, and to obtain data on missing outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek clarification and missing outcome data from study authors; explicitly consider and document the possibility of selective non-reporting of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use funnel plots and related tests to detect small-study effects but interpret cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Funnel plot and related statistical tests can be used to detect ‘small study effect’. However, it is usually impossible to separate the influence of factors other than publication bias on the observed association between the estimated effects and sample sizes across studies in meta-analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow recent recommendations (e.g. Cochrane Handbook) about when and how to use funnel plots/tests; avoid inappropriate interpretation and recognise tests have limited power and may be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitatively assess risk of publication bias using suspected factors and incorporate into conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The risk of publication bias should be qualitatively assessed according to suspected factors associated with publication bias, including small sample size, small effect size, the shape of a funnel plot, the potential number of studies that may have been conducted, conflicting interests of investigators or research sponsors, and any other direct or indirect evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate the estimated risk of publication bias into the review’s conclusions and discuss its potential impact on effect estimates and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use large-scale confirmatory studies when publication bias cannot be excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale confirmatory studies become necessary after a systematic review has reported a clinically significant finding, but publication bias cannot be safely excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When synthesis suggests benefit but risk of dissemination bias remains, recommend or pursue further confirmatory research rather than relying on potentially biased evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise limits and role of trial registers
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials registers will only be helpful in reducing publication bias if systematic reviewers include the registries in their search strategies and results of trials are accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search trial registries and verify accessibility of results; recognise practical difficulties in registering and accessing basic research, observational studies and early exploratory trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply statistical methods for detection/adjustment only as sensitivity analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Many complex statistical methods have been developed to detect or even adjust for assumed publication bias in meta-analysis. More importantly, the usefulness of any statistical methods, simple or complex, may be very limited in typical systematic reviews or meta-analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sophisticated modelling methods primarily for sensitivity analyses rather than to provide a single adjusted estimate; be aware of complexity, lack of user-friendly software and limited empirical validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use electronic publication and open-access databases to reduce bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The recent development of information technology and electronic publication provides great technical potential to overcome some limitations of conventional printed journals. Publication bias may be reduced by publication in electronic media with unlimited space, direct electronic linkage between references, timely publication, and cost-effective dissemination and archiving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage and use electronic and open-access resources maintained by regulators, societies and sponsors to find unpublished or under-reported studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid routine exclusion of grey literature/non-English studies in fields at higher risk (eg complementary medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact of grey literature or studies published in languages other than English may be non-significant in many cases. However, the exclusion of grey literature or non-English-language studies may introduce bias in a systematic review, particularly in the field of complementary medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give special attention to searching for non-English and grey literature in fields where language/grey-literature bias is likely; do not assume non-significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of methodological limitations when studying publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of publication status and classification of study results are often different in empirical studies of publication bias; time to publication can be measured from different points. Bias may be introduced by subjectivity in choice of definitions and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and justify operational definitions (e.g. start point for time-to-publication), assess sensitivity to definitional choices, and interpret study-of-publication-bias findings cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider confounding, selective reporting and generalisability when interpreting evidence about publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Many factors (e.g. sample size, design, research question and investigators’ characteristics) may be associated with both study results and the possibility of publication. Adjusted analyses may be conducted but it is often impossible to exclude the impact of confounding. Single case studies can be biased by selective reporting and generalisability may be limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer evidence from high-quality empirical cohort studies that control for confounding when available; explicitly discuss confounding and generalisability limitations in reviews of publication bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a package of methods to address dissemination biases (Table 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of methods can be used to deal with different types of publication and related bias: prospective registration, right to publication/open access, endorsement of reporting guidelines, disclosure of unpublished studies/data, systematic searching (grey literature, non-English), assessing risk (risk factors, funnel plots/tests), contacting authors, individual patient data meta-analysis, updating reviews and confirmatory studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and document a set of complementary approaches suited to the review question and available resources; some methods target prevention (registration, open access) while others target detection/mitigation (searching, statistical tests, contacting authors).
